utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed -- or, Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber was informed that the Defence wanted to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, and we'll need to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile I use the time for the following. I'd like to say something about the withdrawal of 92 ter motions after the change of the mode of testimony. On the 25th of March, 2015, the Defence filed a motion informing the Chamber that it was changing the mode of testimony for 13 of its witnesses. Instead of calling these witnesses to testify in court, the Defence is planning to present their evidence in written form under Rule 92 bis or Rule 92 quater. The Chamber hereby places on the record that it considers in such and in similar forthcoming circumstances that the corresponding Rule 92 ter motions for such witnesses are also withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Russell, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russell, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Russell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russell, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First I'd like to remind that since we are both speaking English today, we need to try to make a little pause between question and answer so that we don't overlap and we thus permit the court reporter and the translators to do their jobs. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to please state your full name for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: My name is John Henry Russell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can call up 1D03946 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, first of all, sir, do you recognise the statement that we have on the screen for you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes. Could I see also the other pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps with the assistance of the usher, I do have a clean hard copy. If you could show that to the other side first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, sir, I recognise this paperwork with my signature and I remember doing this on the date 17 October 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to the last page of document in e-court so that everyone can see what you're referring to. And we see a signature here. Is that the signature that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And subsequent to the date that is recorded here, have you had an opportunity to review this document in full during proofing to determine if everything is written correctly and accurately therein?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a question about paragraph 37 which is to be found here at the top of the page on page 6. And the second sentence of the paragraph says: "One of our group opened a box and we found 120-millimetre mortars ..." Is this accurate, are we talking about 120-millimetre mortars or something else more specifically?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: We are talking about here 120-millimetre mortar rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And apart from this one clarification in paragraph 37, do you stand behind everything else as written for the remainder of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you questions arising out of the same topics as contained in your written statement, would your answers today be the same as recorded in your statement to those questions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And insofar as you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth today, does that mean that we should consider the answers as written in your statement as being truthful?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would seek the admission of 1D03946 as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D3946 receives Exhibit Number D1219.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would also tender 1D3947 as the associated exhibit mentioned in paragraph 29, footnote number 8, of this exhibit. The others I will be using with the witness so I will only tender one through the statement and the rest will be used in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said 1D3947?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, let me just have a look. Do I ... I find on your list 65 ter 1D03947, and that's indeed, yes, and that has been corrected compared to the initial. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection. And no objection to proceeding as counsel suggests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D3947 receives Exhibit Number D1220.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1220 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would read a short summary of the statement for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: John Russell is a retired major in the Canadian Armed Forces, in which he served from 1970 to 2004 when he retired. On 16 July 1993, he was deployed to the former Yugoslavia as a United Nations Military Observer. On 20 December 1993, he was transferred to Sarajevo to serve as military assistant to Sergio de Mello. He served in that capacity until 28 April 1994. He later returned to the armoured corps in Canada in July 1994. He again served abroad in 2000 and 2001 as a United Nations Military Observer in Syria and Lebanon. On 25 October 1993, while serving as an UNMO in Zadar, he attended a crater analysis training course put on by the United Nations in Knin, Croatia. After arriving in Sarajevo, he was called upon to do crater analysis on several occasions. He also performed crater analysis in southern Lebanon, and showed crater analysis methods to other UN personnel of the team he was with. When he returned to Canada, he provided advice in the preparation of a training scenario on crater analysis at the Canadian Armed Forces Peace Support Training Centre for personnel to be deployed as UNMOs. On 5 February 1994, in Sarajevo, he was tasked to go to the scene of the explosion at the Markale market. He went by himself. At the time, he was not aware the tail fin had been found or that other UN personnel had conducted a crater analysis. When he arrived, he looked for shrapnel but did not find any as the scene had been swept. When examining the crater, he observed the imprint left was smaller than expected. He initially believed the mortar round had struck an object such as a table before hitting the ground. However, after later learning the tail fin had been found embedded in the ground, he determined that round did not strike any object before hitting the ground. He concluded the round had come from east, north-east. He was struck with how steep an angle the round must have come in to clear the large buildings adjacent to the crater. This led him to believe it had come from a location closer to the crater rather than a round fired from farther away. However, based upon the fact that the round could have been fired with zero to six charges, he concluded it was not possible to determine the distance travelled, and since both parties occupied positions in the direction from which the round had come, he could not be certain which side had fired the round. He drafted a report for UNPROFOR Command with his findings and later prepared a second report entitled: "Amplification dealing with the crater analysis of 5 February 1994 at the Sarajevo market" for his boss. Both confirmed his finding that it was impossible to determine with certainty on which side of the confrontation line the round was fired. He recalled hearing a CNN report the evening of 5 February 1994 that the Bosnian Serbs had shelled the market. He believed this was the result of propaganda and that it would be widely believed from then on that the Bosnian Serbs had fired the shell regardless of the facts. He kept a diary. In that diary, he wrote his personal opinion, that he believed the BH shot at themselves. He went on to say: "Many here don't want to think of this, as there are a lot of casualties, but I think otherwise." Some days after the explosion, Major Russell accompanied some UN personnel to the basement of a building in Sarajevo where the Bosniak side kept ammunition. One of the UN personnel had the tail fin recovered from the Markale explosion with him. One of the group found a box of hand-manufactured 120-millimetre mortar rounds that appeared to be welded in the same way as the welding on the tail fin from the market. And this completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Major, I'd like to get some more information about parts of your statement from you. First if we can look together at paragraph 3 on the first page. Here you talk of your deployment as an UN Military Observer first at Zadar and then at Visoko. What was your position in relation to the UNMO structure at each location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Initially in Zadar, I was a new Military Observer, and then within a month I became the deputy team leader, and within that same month I became the team leader of 21 UNMOs from different countries in Team Zadar. When I was assigned in Visoko, in Visoko I was there for one month and I was the OPS officer of Team Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we stay on this page and look at paragraph 4, here you describe your transfer to the role of military assistant to Sergio de Mello. What kind of duties did Mr. de Mello fulfil within his role?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Mr. de Mello was the assistant to the delegate of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now in relation to your own duties while at this position, what did they generally entail?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: As this was a new position, I received direction from Mr. Sergio Vieira de Mello that I would assist him at the highest levels in issues of protection of diplomats or heads of states that would visit Sarajevo, and also assist him in moving deserving people or assisting people that needed maybe medical attention or some other type of attention outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we look at paragraph 8 of the statement, still on the first page, here you talk about the crater analysis and training course in -- while -- while in Knin, I think it is. Can you tell us your recollection of who instructed that course or taught that course.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The course in Knin was conducted at -- in Sector South there. The person conducting the course was a major in the Canadian artillery, and he worked either in Sector South headquarters in Knin or out of Zagreb. I'm not sure which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did anyone else attend this training course?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes. There were at least a dozen - and 12 is the minimum that I can remember - of the other UNMOs in Sector South and also of the battalions that were there, members of the battalions. And I can certainly remember there were at least, as an example, three warrant officers from a Canadian battalion that also participated in that, all of which would find themselves periodically at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now in this paragraph, you state that the course included one half day of actual crater analysis in the field. Could you tell us how this functioned or operated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Well, at the time, that sector was quite active and after the one-day training, the next day we were able to go to actual craters that had hit the ground fresh, I would say fresh, some of them were within three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 9 at the bottom of the page, you identify that you did several crater analyses in addition to the one at Markale market. Can you first tell us the total number of such incidents you had to perform analysis for, and chronologically, did they occur before or after the Markale I?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I did five crater analyses and I believe four of them were before the market one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And by whom would you normally be tasked to do that -- those prior crater analyses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: In -- initially it was with BH command forward in Sarajevo. The Force Commander then would direct his staff to get me to go do some crater analysis. And in the particular case of the market shelling, it was directed from BH command in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these prior crater analyses that you performed, were they before or after you were assigned as military assistant to Mr. de Mello?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: It was at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we turn to the next page of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you did all together some five crater analyses. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at your statement paragraph 9 it says: "I was called upon to do a crater analysis on several occasions. In addition to the Markale market," so Markale market is one, "I recall doing one crater analysis at the Egyptian Battalion," that makes two, "one at the French Battalion," that makes three, "then a few at the airport," which makes at least two, which makes five, "and a few," and I do understand that also to be plural, at least two, "in the streets of Sarajevo." So my total counting brings me to seven. I'm therefore seeking clarification as to why you say five. Or is any of the streets of Sarajevo included -- is Markale market included in that or ... I'm a bit puzzled by the five against the minimum number of seven I count in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only remember five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in your statement and paragraph 10, here you talk of a few crater analyses in southern Lebanon in 2000 through 2001. Can you tell us -- what can you tell us about these analyses that you performed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: One specific incident that I remember was a group of craters that were fired by a 155 battery into an area in south Lebanon to cut off a road for withdrawal type, and those craters were in the field minus of the road, a few were on the road, and a few were plus of the road in the other field. So I saw those as a good opportunity, since they were really good imprints, to teach some of the fellow UNMOs that I was with some crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in the very next paragraph, paragraph 11, you state that you had some role in providing advice to the preparation of training scenarios for personnel to be deployed as UNMOs. What exactly was that role and what kind of advice?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: When I left UNTSO, I was posted back in Canada at the Peace Support Training Centre and there I talked to my commanding officer and I convinced him that one of the things that was lacking in our training was crater analysis. I therefore produced training analysis scenario and displays to show that issue and we introduced that into part of the Military Observer training to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to spend some time talking about your involvement in the Markale market analysis in February of 1994. In paragraph number 12 on this page, you say that you were tasked to go to the scene of the explosion by UN Deputy Commander Ramsey. What precisely were you told had happened prior to going to perform your work at the site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: When I was -- when I found out that I was tasked to go to the market, which I received through a Motorola communication, I was at that time at the Sarajevo airport. I was not aware -- I was aware that an incident had occurred in town but the specifics were not clear to me until I was specifically tasked to go down there and conduct a crater analysis by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the time you were given the assignment, were you told anything about the activity of other UN teams at the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I was totally unaware of any other activity. When I got there, I assumed I was the UN representative doing the crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 14 of the statement that we have in front of us, you say that you got down on one knee to conduct a quick crater analysis. Can you tell us in some more detail what kind of methodology you used to perform this analysis and what kinds of things you were looking for.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: When initially arriving at the site, the first thing I did was I overlooked the site to see if it was safe to go into the site. I then went to the spot where there was the imprint of a round -- a mortar round on the ground. I then conducted a crater analysis first by doing -- trying to determine the direction and I did that by inserting a stake in the middle of the imprint and then in the -- another stake towards the nose furrow. And those two, once they were aligned, I took a bearing on those two and that gave me the general direction from which the round was fired. I measured that, I'd say, about three times to confirm that I was on the right track on the measurements because you're dealing with mils or degrees, in this particular case was mils, and you had to be as precise as you could on that. I then determined the angle of descent, and there is when I found quite interesting that it was the -- the imprint was not that big and that when I was looking at the imprint and I was looking at the direction of where the imprint -- where the indication of the round came from, I kept looking up and up until I reached the top of the -- quite a high building, and I found it quite interesting that only one round had been fired and that it had to be in a steep angle to clear that building to where it landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this method that you utilized at the Markale market on that day in February of 1994, how did it compare to the method that you would normally use to examine mortar craters to determine bearing and angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I did it based on what I learnt in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now looking at page 3 of your statement and paragraph number 20, you state here that you no longer have the measurements you took but you have no reason to doubt those that are recorded in the UN report of 450 mils. I'd like to -- and then you have a footnote for that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at P538 in e-court briefly. And once we get to that document, I'd like to turn to page 9 in the English and page 11 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, here we have a table of results of various UN personnel that measured the crater. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I've seen the one on the right, but I've never seen the one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be the one --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The English one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. And is this -- how does this relate to the report that is referenced in your statement here in paragraph number 20 and 21?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, those are the measurements that I found at the site but I've never seen them in this format until I looked at that particular page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to take look at another part of this document that we have on our screens now, P538. I think it will be page 30 in the English and page 39 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And first of all, to clarify here, under number 7, we see testimony, Sergeant Chief Bouquet, headquarters Sector Sarajevo, and it describes that he led a detachment of soldiers from Sector Sarajevo headquarters tasked to assist in cleaning up the market late on the afternoon of 5 February. His description of the site matches that of other witnesses. He confirmed seeing only one wooden stall surface that showed major effects of the blast and fragmentation. First of all, sir, is this individual's activities at the Markale marketplace at all related with what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page in B/C/S and stay on the same page in English, we see the next entry, number 8, testimony: Major Russell, BH command forward. And you can read here: "During the afternoon of 5 February, Major Russell was at the residency. He was ordered to visit the site by Brigadier Ramsey, COS BH command HQ, and arrived at the market between 1615 and 1630 hours. He walked directly to the site of the crater. There were many reporters in the area, some tables were upset, and he noticed tools - a chisel and a red pipe wrench - within 1 metre of the crater. He saw no shrapnel in the area and concluded that the entire area had been swept thoroughly. He noted that most of the tables (stalls) were intact." Now, do you recall being interviewed and providing this information to someone at the UN?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes. May -- am I allowed to comment, Your Honour, on that statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Ivetic invites you to do so, you can do it but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I comment on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, you may, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. It says in the first sentence "was at the residency." That is my -- where I worked from. On that particular day when I got notified to do this, I was at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And apart from that one correction, does this accurately record the information that you provided to someone at the UN?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, this was a report that was subsequently generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who it would have been who interviewed you to obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: It was at the time, Colonel ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can assist, was he a fellow Canadian --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: He was a Canadian, I just can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Was he a colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yeah, he was a colonel at the time and -- I can't remember his name. I've got a --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. We'll move on. It's not that big of an issue. Now if we could turn to page 50 in English and page --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Joudry. The colonel's name was Colonel Joudry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think you're right. Now if we could turn to page 50 in English and page 69 in the B/C/S, there is another part of this document that bears your name. This fax cover sheet lists you in the upper right and has a signature. First of all, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir. It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now it lists you as the drafter, and then we see some text at the bottom half of the page that says: "Attached please find," and then the rest. Are you the author of this portion of the document as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not the author of the portion below the box, but I am the author of the statement that accompanied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as to who may have prepared the portion that is below the box?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I believe that it was the releasing officer, Major Chretien.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go to the next page in both languages, and looking now at the English original, the second paragraph looks identical to the second -- to the paragraph that you cited in paragraph 15 of your statement as being the memorandum to Mr. de Mello. Is this, in fact, the memorandum that is referenced in paragraph 15 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now in the paragraph marked number 1, you comment that a minimum of three craters will give a better chance of identifying the source than just one. Can you please explain that for us.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: When you fire just one round, normally mortars register their targets. If it's not a registered target, when you fire just one round, then the mortar beds itself or gets in deeper in the ground when it's fired, the mortar base plate. And if you fire a few more rounds, then the base plate gets embedded a bit more, and since mortars are aerial weapons as opposed to precision right-on-the-spot weapons, they have a zone of dispersion. And in this particular case I found that quite unusual to have one round hit a target when I was not aware or found that there was any registration to that particular site and that one round -- three rounds would have been better for more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I can just ask for clarification, you're saying one round hit a target. What was the target? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So we don't know whether this was the target.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Absolutely. So we can't say it hit the target.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, well, it hit the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It hit the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you don't know whether it was the target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also would like to ask one question to clarify. You said you were not aware or found there was any registration to that particular site. What did you do to find out whether there was any such registration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there would have been any previous registration, Your Honour, the UNMO teams on both sides of the confrontation line normally keep track of rounds fired out and the receiving side gets rounds fired in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was: What did you do to find out? Did you check with all of them? Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- seek access to any target lists or ... what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from establishing what we find here that you were not aware.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there were no strikes in the area, no imprints --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but again, I'm asking you what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what -- Your Honour, that's what I'm telling you. When I was there, I was aware there were no other, you know, prints in the general vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean fired on recently or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't find any imprints on the market or at least near to the marketplace and -- so what you did, is you looked around to see whether there were any other imprints.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also, sir, reports from previous firings. There were no such reports on -- available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You inspected them systematically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's then the basis for saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, I was living in Sarajevo, I went up and down those streets all the time. I had a general awareness of what was going on inside the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so that we are clear, you've used the term "registered" or "registering." How does an army operating an indirect fire piece of equipment register a target?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Although I'm not an artillery officer, we worked closely with artillery and the procedure is basically deciding on what target to be hit and then you fire a number of ranging rounds to it, and once you have achieved the desired effect and the closeness to that particular target, you log in your firing log the line and elevation that you used to fire it. And therefore if you need to fire that particular target, it has a number, and you just look at the number, lay down the information, and fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could return to your statement, D1219, and once we get there, if we could look at page 6, paragraph number 38, and here, sir, you say: "Sometime during the week after the explosion, I was interviewed by the UN team commissioned to investigate the Markale shelling." Which interview is at issue here? Is it the one we talked about previously or is it in addition to the one we talked about previously?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying. What number are you looking at here, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 38. Here you talk about an interview by the UN team commissioned to investigate the Markale shelling. You previously told us were interviewed by Colonel Joudry. Is this interview in addition to the interview that you had with Colonel Joudry or is it that same interview?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is the same interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time did the members of the UN team commissioned to investigate the shelling tell you if their conclusions about the potential origin of the round differed from yours?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I don't recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just going to express a little concern right now. The question's been asked, just it's the leading nature. If he talked to them, what did they say, what happened. There's introduction of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would you keep that in mind. Perhaps you rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, the last sentence of your statement says: "I recall being told during the interview that my calculations were closest to the calculations that their team had done." Did they tell you anything else, or what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, that's all that I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you given any figures that were perhaps close to your figures or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know -- there was a time where I didn't know that anybody else had been on the site, and the figures, I saw them when they were in that chart for the first time for comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But during the interview, you didn't see any figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want to turn back to page 3 in your statement and paragraph number 18. In this paragraph, you state that you observed a smaller imprint than you would have expected which led to you believe that the round may have struck a table before hitting the ground. And then in the very next paragraph, paragraph 19, you say based on information that you discovered later, namely that the tail fin had been embedded in the ground, caused you to change that assessment. Now given all that, do you have any other information that would account for the imprint being smaller than you would have expected?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The -- I believed initially that the round had started its initiation of explosion before it hit the ground because the imprint was smaller than normal. But it was bigger, the imprint was bigger than an 82-millimetre mortar that I had done before on some of the other crater analysis. Having found out there was a fin that had been embedded in the grouped and removed, I then determined that I was wrong in that initial assessment and believe that the round actually hit the ground. The size of the crater may have been a result of the steepness of the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you -- what do you exactly understand by imprint? The pattern of damage around the precise point of impact, or the point of impact itself, the size of any -- a hole that may be dug into the ground? What exactly do you understand by imprint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm talking now about the exact imprint, the footprint of that round in the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you -- in terms of size approximately, so it's not the pattern of damage around the impact but the impact itself. But would that include, for example, the small hole that it may dig on impacting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the pattern of that particular round. I'm just talking about when the round hit the ground it makes a print.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Splashing and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is all included in what you say is the imprint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not talking about the material around the market. I'm talking about the round lands and shrapnel escapes the round and makes imprints on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's the whole of the picture that is created by the particles of the projectile visibly later on the ground. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then approximately for a 120-millimetre mortar, what is the -- what do you consider to be the usual imprint and what do you consider to be a smaller than usual imprint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends, Your Honour, on how the round hits the ground. At a lower angle, it spreads more. At a higher angle, it becomes smaller. So the lower the angle, the spread is longer. As you increase the angle this way, the spot on the ground becomes smaller. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's leave it to that for the time being. I mainly was interested to know exactly what you considered to be the imprint. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're at the time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for the first break. Mr. Russell, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom, I'd like to briefly address the following matter. The Defence has recently filed a safe conduct motion in which it, again, requested blanket immunity for its witness and asked that the Chamber orders the Prosecution to refrain from contacting the witness prior to the commencement or after the completion of his testimony. The Chamber has repeatedly reminded the Defence both in court and in its safe conduct orders that there's no basis for these two requests and that the Defence should amend its future safe conduct requests accordingly. The Chamber again invites the Defence to make these changes going forward. Perhaps the copying and pasting should be done very carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to now take a look at 1D03949 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, I also have a hard copy, with the assistance of the usher, that could be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, this document is very similar to the memorandum that we just looked at which was part of P538 except that this one has some handwriting in the paragraph 1 that we just looked at in the other document. Can you please tell us the author or source of this handwritten material?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: These -- that is my writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are you able to, first of all, read for us what is handwritten on this first page, using either the monitor or the hard copy, whichever is easier for you to view.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: It says: "This may no longer be true, but if they came from teams of inspectors. If fin was stuck in the ground, then no above-ground explosion occurred."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: And on the back --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the back, I also wrote: "This would happen anyway."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall -- first of all, in your statement at paragraph number 19, you talk about revising your assessment and making notations on that document. Is this the document that you referenced in paragraph number 19 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And apart from these written modifications you have made to your memorandum, do you still stand behind the conclusion that either side could have been responsible for the mortar that landed that day in Markale market?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at this time, Your Honours, we would tender this document, 1D03949, as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The version with handwritten notations, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it true there is no B/C/S translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, B/C/S translation would serve us to have on paper also the text which was read by the witness. Now, usually I don't have great concerns about the B/C/S translation, but here where it may not be too easy to read it, perhaps we should insist on a B/C/S translation, Mr. Ivetic. I hope you understand that it's mainly to avoid whatever misunderstandings in the future, especially in terms of the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honours. And as I understand CLSS's position, I can only seek a B/C/S translation of a document once Your Honours order me to get one, so that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think under the present circumstances that would be -- the Chamber would insist on having a translation in B/C/S. Not that much in relation to the typewritten text but mainly in relation to the handwriting. Madam Registrar, would you please give a number under which this document will be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D3949 receives Exhibit Number D1221, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. You'll inform the Chamber once the B/C/S translation is uploaded, Mr. Ivetic, after you have verified that the handwritten portions are appropriately dealt with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can briefly look at 65 ter number 19771 and page 5 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, this comes from a series of documents -- photographs, pardon me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, I would have some objection to the counsel educating the witness as to what is depicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you ask the witness what he thinks he sees on the photograph, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this photo before I showed to you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see anything at Markale market similar to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this a bit leading, or very leading, or the most leading, Mr. Ivetic? Would you please refrain from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there any marking around the imprint of the crater shell that you analysed at the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Well, first, Your Honour, I don't recognise this picture. Second of all, when I did my crater analysis, there was a lot of blood, a lot of garbage, a lot of stuff around there, and there were no white marks like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there anything embedded in the furrow tunnel of the imprint that you looked at on the day that you examined the Markale market crater?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suspect, Mr. Ivetic, the correct way to ask the question is: What did you find? Not: Was there anything embedded? Otherwise you're suggesting that there was something embedded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we're dealing with a witness who has given a statement as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is true and he told us what he found.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So to further say to him something was embedded is to introduce something to his mind which he hasn't commented upon on his own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I don't think that I'm suggesting that anything was embedded. I'm asking him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you asked the question: Was there anything embedded? That's the question you put.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What did you find in the furrow tunnel of the imprint that you examined on Markale market on -- in February of 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: When I looked at the imprint, I found disturbed ground, the imprint itself, and then I proceeded to conduct a crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you make any drawing of the shape of the crater?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you proceeded to conduct your crater analysis, did you have to examine the fuse furrow tunnel created by the impact of the mortar round on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I, first of all, looked for a fuse nose cone and I didn't see any, and then I proceeded in conducting the crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at this time we would mark this photograph for identification. I think we only need this one in relation to the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think the witness has offered any comments of substance that necessitate even marking this exhibit at this time. If counsel intends to use it with another witness that might have more knowledge, they can be -- feel free to do so at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this is a Prosecution document that has been represented as pertaining to the site and it's for illustrative purposes only. When we say: Did you see something marked this way, the only way we can know that is by looking at the photograph to depict what is marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The Chamber considers that we would better understand the testimony of this witness if this document would be in evidence. He said what he didn't see, for example, and then it's always good to know what was shown to him. Therefore, and for -- and I have one additional question. Mr. Weber, you -- Mr. Ivetic claimed that this is a photograph provided by the Prosecution and is related to the Markale market incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm trying to avoid any confusion on the record and I understand Your Honours' ruling. If that's the case, then actually we do have obviously a lot of other evidence admitted related this event. I'd actually ask that all photographs be admitted, then, so we could properly associate it to the rest of the materials and the timing and sequence of the various investigations that happened, and not just an individual photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, a problem would be that if the witness then tells us that he doesn't recognise all that, then it doesn't bring us much further, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. And I can tell you in relation to this Prosecution 65 ter number, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if you think it would assist the Chamber where the link as established now between the knowledge of the witness and the photograph shown to him is sufficient to -- for us to admit, then you can tender all of the other documents in cross, if you wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll proceed as the Chamber wishes. I believe this witness has been clear about his absence of knowledge and having seeing these before. But we do have, for example, videos in evidence so that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's a different matter. But in order to know what the witness doesn't recognise, it's -- we need to have it either marked for identification or in evidence. There is no dispute about this being related to the 5th of February incident at the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, although I think it is unclear as to the chronology of when this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- so I understand Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that the witness can't help us with that any further, Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think he can, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I leave it to you to -- otherwise the link, of course, is not the strongest you could imagine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask a question for clarification. Mr. Russell, do you, as you sit here, have a recollection of the shape of the crater as you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in detail, Your Honour, but I remember it was just a bloody hole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand the blood. But -- I mean, I'm talking about the shame.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's -- it was the shape that I would have expected from a mortar round, you know, with the splattering marks of shrapnel on the -- on the pieces of -- on the ground, but that's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm really talking about the hole itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there's always a hole and there's always stuff in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Can you remember the shape of that hole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1222, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1222 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought it was MFI so we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- get only that picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then it's marked for identification awaiting for the upload of this one and only picture. Mr. Weber, if you want to tender them all, then rather say it now that we keep them together, but apparently you are not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we could turn to your written statement, which has been marked now as D1219, and look at paragraph 24 and 25 of the same to be found on page 4, and here you are talking about the depth of the hole and the effect of reinsertion of the tail-fin. In relation to this part of your statement, you were asked in the Karadzic case about this, and I'm about to read a selection from that transcript to you that starts at transcript page 29392, line 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't see the Karadzic transcript as part of the 92 ter materials, and I think that it's just been the practice. We have elicited the evidence anew when matters that were in other transcripts were not being offered as part of the 92 ter materials, we've just a led it in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not part of the 92 ter materials, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't think we've ever tendered transcripts from other proceedings unless they're pursuant to Rule 92 ter or 92 bis. The Prosecution has used Sanction. I don't have Sanction, but I do have the ability to show it if we could turn on the Defence monitor. I do have the relevant transcripts on the screen and you can follow along as we have done in the court for other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Weber mentioned something else, that was that the Prosecution was not notified that you would use it. The Prosecution uploaded a part of the transcript from another case as a new 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I beg to differ with counsel. If he looks at the bottom of the list, he will see that the transcript is indeed listed as prior testimony for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I do understand it's a part of my list. My concern even more --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's part of my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- more beyond this is that it -- I'm concerned about where we're going here. It's a form of leading and proceeding this way where we're bringing up the transcript in this manner. I understand I can do that on cross-examination, but it's counsel's obligation, I believe, at this time, to open-ended ask the witness questions if it stems from the statement that tendered pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can be fairly open with what I'm going to do. I am going to present what was discussed with Prosecution counsel in the Karadzic case, and I'm going to ask an open-ended question in relation to that which he testified about in that case in this paragraph, that will be completely open-ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I think new for me is that you wanted to quote parts of the cross-examination or was that ... I think it was not clear to me -- does that change in any way your mind, Mr. Weber, that it will be the OTP questions that will be put to the witness, and then I take it that you'll seek either confirmation or denial of the accuracy of those answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: One, right now I don't actually know what is going to be asked but I don't think that would be proper to do because he's leading the witness at that time. Counsel is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you want a witness to either confirm or deny a previous statement, then it's good that he knows -- or a testimony about what kind of questions put to you. But if you insist, the Chamber has been relatively liberal in allowing the parties to put to a witness what he testified in other cases. I also tend to agree with you that that is -- more often was done in cross-examination, although not exclusively, I think. If you insist, then we'll ask Mr. Ivetic, he can read the questions that were put by you and seek an answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've stated our position and I defer to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're perfectly free to put a question which is the same or similar to a question put by the OTP in another case to the witness. But in view of the objections, you are supposed not to give the witness an opportunity to look at his answers or read them to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then let me do the open-ended question I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, after being cross-examined by the Prosecution as to paragraphs 24 and 25 of your statement, do you have anything that you wish to change as to paragraph 24 and 25 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would need time to read them, Witness, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the statements on 24 and 25 are the ones that I have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you stand by -- and do you stand by those?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving along to paragraph 27 of your statement, and this is to be found on the same page, page 4, you say that speed that a round hits the ground has never been an issue. Can you tell us, sir, what does it's training in crater analysis that is provided by the UN or the Canadian army have to say about taking into account the speed of a round hitting the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: It was the UN, not the Canadian army that I took the training from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: And in that training, the speed at which the round hits the ground was not considered. We were just considering the direction and angle of descent. And in my previous example of the crater analysis I did in Lebanon, all the rounds that landed in the field were deeper in the ground than the rounds that landed on the road. That's all I have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you what triggered you to make this observation in paragraph 27?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was based on the Prosecution asking about the depth, did I measure it, and I said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you gave your statement, you had been interviewed already by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was. I was proofed by the Prosecution in the other trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see, you gave this statement, if I see it well, on the 17th of October, 2011.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's when I wrote it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You had been proofed by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came in October of 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see: "Prior to being interviewed by Peter Robinson on the 12th of October, I had never been contacted by anyone from the ICTY. The interview with Mr. Robinson was conducted in the presence of Major Marla Dow of the Canadian Armed Forces." Where were you interviewed by Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kingston, Ontario, sir, in Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when then -- you said you were proofed by the Prosecution prior to giving this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was -- this statement existed and when I came in 2012, the day before I testified, the Prosecution proofed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we had a discussion about the crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay, that's all fine. But I asked you what triggered paragraph 27 in your statement. And you said: I was asked by the Prosecution, but you had no spoken with the Prosecution yet when you gave that statement. So, again, my question is: What triggered you to say something about the speed and that in your experience it had never been an issue? What triggered that observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. It could be Mr. Robinson asking me: Did you consider the speed? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a look together at paragraph 32 on page 5 of your statement, here you talk of hearing on CNN the evening of 5 February 1994 that the Bosnian Serbs had shelled the market. Do you know if anyone on the UN side had made such a determination by that date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the remainder of this paragraph of your statement, you state you believed this was the result of propaganda and that from then on, it would be widely believed the Bosnian Serbs had fired the shell regardless of the true facts. Whose propaganda did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Whoever had the most to gain from the particular comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would not be the first question: What is the basis of your belief, to have a foundation for what is presented here as belief rather than a personal observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard the question offered by the Honourable Judge. Are you able to answer that question? What is the basis for your belief that this was the result of propaganda? The statement on CNN.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: There's always a -- everyone's in a hurry to find out who did it, Your Honour. And the UN had not yet passed on the information they received on those crater analysis to make it official, but the news media was saying something and I don't know where they got it. So that's all I'm saying based on that is, the -- to the best of my knowledge, at that time, that evening, the reports from the crater analysis from all of us was in the hands of the UN chain of command and had not been released to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it was a conclusion of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I could see the TV said someone did it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- I see that. But that it was propaganda was [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a conclusion, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a conclusion. And then perhaps the next question, whose propaganda it was, did you form any opinion about that? Was it CNN making propaganda or someone who fed the CNN with that information or any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer to that, Your Honour, is whoever had the most to gain from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to paragraphs 33 through 35 of your statement, you reference a diary. Before we get to those specific parts of your statement, I'd like to ask you about the diary. Was there a specific reason that you had for keeping a diary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: In the Canadian Peace Support Operations training, one of the things we train is to keep a diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could take look at 1D03948 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, what we have on the screen now, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting, and that's the pages in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "that's the pages in my diary," in relation to the selections identified in paragraph 33 and 35 of your statement, how do these pages correlate to those selections?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: They are an accurate reflection of what my opinion was, what I thought of when I wrote it, based on those numbers you just -- paragraphs you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this and leave it up to Your Honours if we need a B/C/S translation of this. We can do it the same way as the last document if you so order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the parties would agree on what is written here, then -- and that might even be a solution for the other matter as well, perhaps a more simple one, without the need to have CLSS prepare a translation. And, Mr. Ivetic, irrespective of what I said earlier, perhaps you could seek an agreement with Mr. Weber on the accuracy of the handwritten text at the UN report. Is there any way the parties could agree on the content of what's written here in the English language?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that we can on both matters. I do find that this document is legible, and I believe the witness did correctly read in the handwriting from the earlier document into the record. With respect to the tendering of this particular document, we did agree to proceed today with respect to the diary. We had asked for the more complete version, but I believe this is just a matter of potential weight for the document. And we do have a concern that this -- these diary entries are potentially incomplete. For example, on page 164 it doesn't appear to be the complete page, nor from page 165. So with that being said, we just express that reservation and not articulate any further specific objection to the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, the incompleteness of the pages seems not to be the major concern of the Prosecution, but the Chamber would like to know what portions of a page it receives. If it is all about the same day. I mean, what's the reason for perhaps not presenting the full pages, if these are not the full pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can answer that. I'm presenting what was presented in the Karadzic case and which I have access to. I don't have access to the full diary. This witness has been presented to us by the Rule 70 provider and the Rule 70 provider has not granted me access to the whole diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you asked for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I communicated the Prosecution's request for the whole diary to them, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, is it Rule 70 procedure which deprives of us looking at the full pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Defence that is the proponent of the material and I properly made a Rule 67 request. And I believe it is incumbent upon them as the tendering party to produce material that they're seeking to provide, and I think that in that context there is no Rule 70 aspect with respect to us. And yes, last Thursday, I was informed by Mr. Ivetic that our Rule 67 request to the Defence related to a document they're seeking to tender into evidence was forwarded to the Canadian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit puzzled by the present situation. There are Rule 70 restrictions that do apply? Not as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who received the material from the Canadian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe it's the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Karadzic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, you're presenting it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- and what exactly are the Rule 70 restrictions imposed on the Karadzic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The excerpted diary that was presented and used without any objection to the Prosecution in the Karadzic case is the same document that we have now on our screen. In talking with the Canadian authorities, they reminded me that I don't have a complete version of the diary and that I -- that they were not in a position to give it to me, but they invited the Prosecution to make a formal request of them and they would consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you asked the Karadzic Defence whether they received a full copy of the pages 163, 164, and 165?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Prior to this testimony, no. But I believe previously when I did discuss -- this is a document that we obviously received in disclosure from the Karadzic case. This is the associate exhibit to this Karadzic statement that we're using with this witness, so we did not create anything new or upload anything new. We just transferred the exact same documents to our e-court and they obtained new numbers in our system at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently you were satisfied by incomplete pages. Let's see whether the Chamber also is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's in itself the reason not admit. Therefore, we'll admit it. But the Chamber is seeking the full pages to the extent relevant and invites the parties to see to what extent and where they can get it. And if they need the assistance of the Chamber, the Chamber will certainly assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then we'll need to involve the UN headquarters in New York and the Canadian authorities who have been the ones that are -- that provided the permissions to bring this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is that the reason not to be interested into the totality of it? You seem to be desperate already. As I said, the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm far from desperate, Your Honours. I'm just providing helpful information to the Chamber so you have the full picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We said the Chamber would assist the parties in getting access to the entire pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I note that with Prosecution witnesses -- RM507, Your Honours did not make any efforts to make those Rule 70 providers provide material to us that they did not deem that we should have, so I'm a little concerned about inequalities of treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Forgive me for not remembering exactly what you are referring to. I will do that after this court session. What I see here and our attention was drawn to the fact that on the three pages apparently covering that one date, that parts of the pages are missing, and the Chamber is always interested in context. But I'll -- the Chamber will verify the references you made and to see to what extent they are helpful for us in drawing the same lines for both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you have any information whether or not the Karadzic Defence had the entire or -- diary or even some more pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do, but think the witness has the better knowledge of that and so I'll let the witness answer Your Honour's question, if you would permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give us information, what did the Karadzic Defence receive? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I was asked to look in my diaries to see if I had any entries. These are the only entries that deal with the issue that I'm here today. You can see in one of the pages that stuff is blacked out. It has nothing to do with why I'm here. The other parts are parts of pages, Your Honours, that deal specifically, underlined in yellow, with this issue here. The rest of it has nothing do -- the whole rest of the diary has nothing do with the issue here at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you make this selection personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I underlined in yellow so I would be able to refer to it fast, and then photocopied them, and then provided them to the Defence at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You provided --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- those portions and you made the selection yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I knew where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was any instruction given to you as what to include and what not include by your government or any other agency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had -- it was your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did this myself. I looked, okay, at 2/09, that day, 7th of February, on page 164, that's the only thing that has anything to do with why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I hope you'll understand that these are -- what is relevant and what is not relevant is often determined by the Chamber and, of course, we carefully listen to what witnesses tell us but finally it's our determination. Now, it may be for the full 100 per cent true, you say, but perhaps you're not entirely in a position to -- to know exactly what is relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. But I received the piece of paper that said there is other things in my diary that could be sensitive information that no other people should know based on what I did, whether for Mr. de Mello or from my own personal family. Therefore, my understanding is that my diary is my diary. And when I provided the information, I was asked to provide anything I knew or had and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you directly provided it to the Karadzic Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. Directly -- I had to go through my country, right? I had to go through all those requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we know where we are. Do you still have the full diary in your possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At home, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please keep it carefully so that if there's any need to provide any further pages that -- that it's there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that for the time being. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D3948 receives Exhibit Number D1223, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1223 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
