utterances.text: Now if we could return to your statement, which is D1219, page 5, and I'd like to focus on the last half of paragraph 33 -- or I should say, the last half of the entry from 5 February 1994 from your diary that is recorded in this paragraph, where it says: "I was at the site to do a quick crater analysis and although I agree with the direction that the round came from, I disagree with the distance, believing that the BiH shot at themselves. "Many here don't want to think of this as there are a lot of casualties, but I think otherwise." To whom were you referring when you said "many here don't want to think of this as there are a lot of casualties"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: My colleagues in general at BH command. They found it unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what is it actually you disagree with? Because you're talking of believing that the BiH -- what is it that you disagree with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I disagreed with my -- this is my personal opinion in my diary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but what is it you are disagreeing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I disagreed with the -- in my diary, in the minimum/maximum range. I believe that the range was within the confrontation line on the BiH side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could I then ask you, you said saying on the 5th of February in the evening that the shell was fired from the Serb side is propaganda because -- and that's what you elsewhere say in your statement as well, you're unable to make up whether it was from the one side of the confrontation line or the other side. Now, apparently on the 5th of February, you had made up your mind as that it did not come from the Serb side but did come from the BH side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's what I wrote in my diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at the same time, you say that you couldn't know whether it was fired from the one side or the other side. Do you have any explanation as to -- and perhaps I take you to the ... You quoted in paragraph 29 a report saying that: "The crater analysis carried out showed that the shell could have been fired from either BiH or Serb positions." And then in paragraph 30 you say: "This accurately reflects the official conclusions that I reported to my superiors on the 5th of February, 1994." And a little bit further down you say: "It's therefore impossible to determine with certainty on which side of the confrontation line the round was fired." Now in paragraph 32 you say CNN, that's propaganda, because you -- they couldn't know. And then in your own diary, you come to believe that it was BiH who shot at themselves. Could you explain to us why in all your reporting you say you can't know, why you say if you -- if it comes from the Serb side, that's propaganda, and then tell us that on the 5th of February, you believed that it came from within the confrontation line and not from the BiH side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The official crater analysis report that I did and the findings that I had determined that I could not prove who did it. And based on the direction and the angle of descent that I had, that I thought was it, I still was not convinced on which side did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, therefore, in my conclusion, I concluded that between charge 1 and 6 covered the whole of the confrontation line to which the two fighting factions were involved, and, therefore, I could not in my investigation say who did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But why then do you write in your diary on that same day that you believed that the BiH shot at themselves? Or is this just a kind of a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because in my personal opinion, when I was at the site and I looked at the angle of descent personally, I looked at that, and I believed in my own opinion that said that that round came from a shorter range than a longer range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you did that on the basis of the -- of the buildings or just kind of an overall impression --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, because the angle was steep. The angle was not like this, it was like this. It was steep and I felt personally, in my diary, and I wrote it only in my diary, that this is what I felt. But in the official UN documentation, Your Honours, I could not determine who did it and therefore my official answer was that I could not determine who fired this round because from the minimum to the maximum range, it could have been on any side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it was a subjective feeling, looking around --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's my opinion, in my diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to look at paragraph number 36 of the statement. In the footnote to paragraph 36, you say that you are not listed as part of the delegation but you were invited and went along. Could you please tell us how it was that you became a part of this visit or how you accompanied this delegation that performed this visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: So when Sector Sarajevo decided to do this particular investigation, one of the members of that team was the team leader of the UNMOs in Sector Sarajevo, a Canadian, a major. He knew I worked in BH command forward. He knew I had done a crater analysis, and so I was invited, and the leader of that team apparently had no objection. I am not -- excuse me. I am not marked as one of the investigation teams in that particular group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall in what kind of building that basement was that we are talking about that was located on the Bosniak side in Sarajevo that is discussed in paragraph 36?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I recall we went to a high-rise building in the middle of Sarajevo. It was a civilian-occupied building with a military component, I believe, on the first bottom three floors. And from there, we went to the basement. Well, after -- after interviewing the person in charge there by that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page of your statement and look at paragraph 37 of the same, and here you describe interviewing the person in charge and then how you -- how one of the group opened a box and found 120-millimetre mortars. How did you examine these 120-millimetre mortars that were found?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Now, here we're talking about the 100-millimetre rounds, not the mortar -- not the firing --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You're correct, sir. I meant rounds.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I held one in my hands and I was particularly interested in the -- in the fin part, how it was manufactured, and so I looked at the complete round. And then the fin was there and we looked at it, and I found that the welding on the fins appeared to be the same. And that's what I concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about the colour or appearance of this mortar round which in your statement you say were hand manufactured?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: They were like polished -- you know, like silver or chrome -- not chrome. Polished metal and, you know, made on a lathe or whatever, to make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss your observations as to the similarity in welding with any of the other persons from the UN that were present?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I just pointed it out to my colleague, the Canadian UNMO chief in Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to take a look briefly at P797 in e-court. And if we can turn to page 6 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I guess do have an objection related to the use of this document. The witness, according to the statement, left and went back to Canada in July 1994 and this material and investigation relates to something that he was just not part of -- or that related to Markale II, so at this point in time I would object to the use of this. It's also outside the notice in terms of the time-period in which counsel put us on notice for prior to the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe everyone received a proofing note yesterday that I sent out after meeting with the witness that identified this document. I'm -- I haven't even asked the question yet, so I don't know to what extent there can be an objection before I phrased the question. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is against the use of the document before the witness, Mr. Ivetic. It's not an objection against the question but against the use of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have notified the party that I was going to use the document and I believe it has some relevance to assist the Chamber if I were to ask one question about it that doesn't go to the truth of the document or any of the facts as to this particular time-period, but rather a description in the document. And again it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just add that the only comment that is in the proofing note is: "The Defence amends the exhibit list and adds to the exhibit for this witness the document P797." That doesn't place us on notice of anything in terms of substance that might be led through the witness or what the witness may know in relation to this document or may comment upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the way the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- does this all the time, I can pull up 15 e-mails --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- where they just list numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Accepted. Let's wait for the question, Mr. Weber. But, Mr. Ivetic, if the question can be put to the witness first on any subject matter without showing the document to him, that's what you're supposed to do. And only in second instance, if there's no way to ask what you would like to elicit from the witness other than by showing him the document, then in the second round you can do so. That's the -- I think, the standard which was mainly applied --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honours. And considering that he was not in Sarajevo at the time of this document's generation, the only way I can ask him about something in the document is by showing it to him since I can't elicit -- I can't ask him out of the blue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this is -- of course you can't. I've not heard the question yet. But the idea that you can't -- if a witness wasn't there, that you can't put a question to him which is relevant without showing a document is, of course, not -- in its general sense not true. But let's first hear your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this document that we have before us, Lieutenant-Colonel Mougey, writing for Sector Sarajevo, has recorded for this particular instance in the last full paragraph: "This munition is of Serb manufacture, being unmarked and unpainted with a brushed steel finish, which matches current Bosno-Serb war design." How does this description of this round in this report compare to your recollection of the round you just described to us which you held in your hands in the basement of the building in Sarajevo in 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you answer that question, Witness. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. Foundation. Basis of knowledge. The counsel is asking the witness to compare something that is a part of another investigation. There's much more detail and information obviously about the round, what it was, how it was marked and finished, with respect to this incident. And right now there's just no foundation for this witness even knowing about this other incident for which -- him to give any type of comparison or at this point just out-right opinion about the shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is based on my description of the round that I held in my hands and when I said it looked like a silver coating or whatever, is that it was unmarked and unpainted, and the brushed steel finish that is mentioned in that document is another way of saying what I said. That's all I have to comment on that particular thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question, sir. The one that you -- that you're talking about in your -- in your statement, do you know where it came from, the origin of that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It came from the basement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- on the BiH side in a wooden box. That's all I know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It is not alleged to be what was found at Markale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- in the years since you first performed your crater analysis has anything caused you to change your conclusions about the possible origin of the mortar round that struck the market in February 1994, or do you still believe it is not possible to confirm with certainty which side of the confrontation line that round came from as stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: My position has not changed from the statement in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Major, I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all the questions I had for the witness. I do think we're at the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are at the time for a break. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You'll then be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. Therefore, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russell, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You'll find Mr. Weber to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major Russell.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We've heard that you previously testified in the Karadzic case. Did you tell the truth during your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In regards to paragraph 37 of your statement, is it your suggestion that these mortar shells that you found in the basement were from the same lot of mortars that were fired upon the Markale market on 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, it is not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That is not your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You believed --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I only commented on I thought that the welding of the fin of that round looked like the welding of that famous fin that people found there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Russell, when Mr. Ivetic started your examination, he reminded you to pause between question and answer. This applies to Mr. Weber as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no problem. Mr. Weber, I don't know whether the welding will be something you would like to continue in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a couple of more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In answer to your last question I'm not quite sure I heard it properly and it doesn't look like it's correctly recorded: "The only thought that the welding of the fin of that round looked like that famous fin that people found there." Is that what you said, Mr. Russell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Famous.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Major Russell, I'm going to try to slow down a little bit too. You believe the shells in the basement were handmade because, one, they had no identification marks; two, they appeared roughly made on a lathe; three, they had a free-floating firing pin at the front?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You knew that the shells were roughly made on a lathe because when you picked it up, it had all the rough edges on it, unlike a manufactured round; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct. It had -- you know how it had little lines all around it? You know how it goes through a lathe and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You are aware that the stabilizer found at the market-place on the 5th of February did have identification marks on it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: From the reports I read on it, I understand that there was numbers on the back of the fin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, and I know you're not familiar with the other investigation you were just shown, you're also not suggesting that there was some similarity between the mortar that you looked at in the basement and ones that might have been recovered a year, year and a half after your departure from -- from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct. I'm only talking about words. You know, descriptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for those clarifications. I'm going to eventually come back to events on the 5th of February, but I'd like to go through some things more generally first. You were in Sarajevo from the 20th of December, 1993, until the 28th of April, 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I was there three and a half months, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have I accurately stated those dates?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: If they're stated in this particular piece of paper, you are correct, those are the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Now with respect to your duties in relation to Mr. de Mello, you would attend meetings with him; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Sometimes I would, and sometimes I'd be away arranging logistics for future meetings or the same meeting or as a result of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 03437 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a memorandum from Mr. de Mello to Mr. Akashi, dated 4 January 1994, related to a meeting with Radovan Karadzic. In the first paragraph of the memo, it refers to a meeting on 3 January in Pale with Dr. Karadzic and Mr. de Mello indicates he was accompanied by you. This is an example of the types of meetings you would attend with Mr. de Mello; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: This is the one meeting there that I attended and specifically there. It was over a lunch, a working lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was anyone else present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No -- just the three of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please pause before you start answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph number 2, Mr. de Mello indicates he listed a series of incidents which that very morning had brought UNPROFOR to near paralysis. And then there is reference to cumulative petty harassment in contravention of agreements concluded or signed with Karadzic, General Mladic or General Milovanovic. Could you tell us about these particular incidents that were mentioned on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I was there at the lunch for the purpose of Mr. de Mello introducing me to the key players in the region and to observe how things operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Major Russell, I'm going to focus your attention on paragraph 7. In paragraph number 7, under the section entitled: "Shelling in retaliation to firing from BiH area of Sarajevo," Mr. de Mello states in the first sentence: "I again pointed out to Karadzic that UNPROFOR monitors all shooting in and out of Sarajevo, that there are records kept as to who fired first, and that we have been very objective in our reporting, including to the press, which he again acknowledged." I'm just going to stop here before going on to the next sentences. In the sentence there is reference to this again being pointed out. Can you tell us of any previous occasions Mr. de Mello pointed out this information to Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, to the best of my knowledge, this was the time that I was with him that he mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. This information in the sentence is accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: This is Mr. de Mello who wrote this. I didn't write it. And I would assume that it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The next sentence states: "Disproportionate scale of retaliation to small levels of firing, however, served no military purpose, caused tragic civilian casualties, and was highly detrimental to the Serb image and cause." Did you personally observe disproportionate Serb shelling that served no military purpose while you were in Sarajevo? You must have seen that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: While in Sarajevo I observed a lot of shelling from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, based on your answer, we're then going to look at a number of other documents. The last part of this paragraph indicates that Karadzic agreed the retaliation was inappropriate and unproductive and said he would discuss the matter with General Galic. He also pointed out that the BiH was launching fierce ground attacks from inside Sarajevo. Could you tell us if you know at any other point in time, did Mr. de Mello convey these same concerns to anyone in the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, Mr. de Mello didn't deal with the army. He dealt with the political level. I can certainly tell you that after this meeting, that Mr. de Mello met Mr. Izetbegovic at the airport and talked to him about the meeting of which I don't know what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- Mr. Weber, could I take the witness back to one of your previous questions although it's not fully recorded. Mr. Weber asked you about whether you observed -- and perhaps, Mr. Weber, you fill in what you said at page 61, line 24, could you please read what you said there. Just the portion which is left out? "Did you permanently observe ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I don't think that's what I read out. I think I asked "did you personally observe."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. "Did you personally observe," and I take it then it's shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Disproportionate Serb shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Did you personally observe disproportionate Serb shelling that served no military purpose while you were in Sarajevo?" Your answer was: "While in Sarajevo, I observed a lot of shelling from both sides." But that wasn't the question. The question was whether you observed, whether you personally observed, disproportionate Serb shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I would say no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, Mr. Weber actually asked a different question. He said: "You had to have seen that," was the second part of that question [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was not a question but it was apparently a statement. That's the reason why I did not repeat that because I prefer to ask questions rather than to make statements. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03437 receives Exhibit Number P7534, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32826 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you verify whether it's uploaded, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you to the court officer and to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Major Russell, I'm now going to go through the UNMO Sector Sarajevo sitreps coinciding with the arrival -- your arrival in Sarajevo. I would like to draw your attention to the first sitrep that's before you. It is from the 19th to the 20th of December, 1993. The general assessment includes information on fighting in the western part of the city and other residential areas shelled, including the city centre, Sedrenik, Grahoviste, and Hrasnica. There is information on the death of one child. And we see -- I just want to get in the process of looking at these because we're going to look at a number of them. Under section 2 on page 2 of the B/C/S, the UNMOs confirmed 197 mixed impacts incoming and zero outgoing from Bosnian-held areas. They also confirmed 141 mixed rounds outgoing and two incoming to Serb-held areas. Sir, do you recall the fact that this was the level of shelling around the time that you arrived -- first arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the sitrep for the 20th and -- to 21st December 1993. We see that there is heavy shelling on this date. In section 1, the sitrep indicates artillery and mortar positions on the high ground to the west and north of the city were active. We see the residential areas that were shelled. 26 were wounded, two by sniper, and six killed on the Bosnian side, and four wounded and one killed on the Serb side. We see that they also include a little bit more information on the day before. Overall, on this day, UNMOs confirmed 1.502 mixed impacts incoming and 17 outgoing from Bosnian-held areas, and 1.259 outgoing rounds and 17 mixed impacts in Serb-held areas. This is quite a heavy shelling. Does this help you recall what the level of shelling was like when you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Well, I remember, what I recall is that there was on this particular date there -- and when you mentioned the number, I remember, yes, that was a high number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under section 4 of this same sitrep, we see that UNMOs were restricted in movement in the areas of Rajlovac, Lukavica, and the Pale road. While you were in Sarajevo, Bosnian Serb forces restricted the movement of UNMOs; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do note this goes beyond the scope of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm permitted pursuant to 90(H) to inquire with respect to this witness, and with respect to the scope of examination, the witness in response to Mr. Ivetic's questions even indicated that his opinions that he was offering this Court were based on his time in Sarajevo. So I think the -- that counsel clearly triggered this and I'd -- anyway it would be fair for me to inquire about it under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If counsel triggered for it, I'd like for him to cite in the transcript where I asked about anything apart from shellings and the investigation that this witness did and about any kind of -- these types of incidents which I did not ask about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, the cross-examining party is limited to issues raised during chief to any matter that may assist its case and credibility issues. And the Chamber considers that the questioning until now does not go beyond that. The objection, therefore, is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I see you answered the previous question. I'll move on. Under section 14, the sitrep indicates that this period between the 20th and 21st was the highest level of shelling in the past two months. Were you aware that there was a significant increase in Bosnian Serb shelling right when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I was not aware of increased shelling. But that commander's statement 14, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 4 of the English original and page 7 of the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the sitrep for the 21st to 22nd of December, 1993. On this date, UNMOs confirmed 1.744 mixed impacts incoming and eight outgoing mortars from Bosnian-held areas, and 1.060 outgoing rounds and 244 explosions heard from Serb-held areas. In the first section the sitrep also indicates many residential areas were shelled, including the city centre, Sedrenik, and parts of the old city. We see the UNMOs confirmed one killed and 12 wounded, two critical, with an ongoing investigation into additional killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just maybe so we expedite this, could the Prosecution please have page 6 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please indicate sections from which he is reading for the purposes of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the sitrep for the 22nd to the 23rd of December, 1993. On this date, UNMOs confirmed 1.309 mixed impacts incoming and 14 outgoing mortars from Bosnian-held areas, and 1.557 outgoing rounds and 95 impacts in Serb-held areas. This can be found in section 2. The sitrep indicates above in section 1 that many residential areas were again shelled along with areas close to the confrontation line, including Dobrinja. We see that there are 68 persons wounded and five killed on the Bosnian side. And now that we've gone through these first three dates after your arrival, I'd really like to ask you what were your impressions like when you experienced this level of shelling when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Hot. There's a lot of shelling. But are you asking me this as a Military Observer or as the MA to Mr. de Mello? Because those are two different jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 7 of the English and page 12 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, in order to avoid any misunderstandings, I think that Mr. Weber asked you about your impression when you arrived, irrespective of what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a lot of shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said: Are you asking this as a Military Observer or as what you observed irrespective of whatever function you were at the time. You said there was a lot of shelling. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand what he said ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a sitrep for the 23rd to the 24th of December, 1993. In the first section, we see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged in the English version, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We see in the first section that the residential areas were shelled, includes "the city centre, as always." The UNMOs on this date did not observe any ground fighting. There were 30 persons wounded and two killed on the Bosnian side. UNMOs confirmed 784 mixed impacts incoming and four outgoing mortars from the Bosnian-held areas, and 360 outgoing rounds and 113 impacts in Serb-held areas. This information is in section 2. Based on the sitreps we just looked at, there was a total of 5.536 impacts on the Bosnian side between the 19th and 24th of December. Sir, this is, in fact, disproportionate shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for a legal conclusion. This witness is here as a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness has expressed himself on many, many issues, drawn conclusions, et cetera. The question is whether you considered this disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 32826 into evidence. In fairness, the Prosecution has included the last few sitreps from the days towards the end of the month where the shelling subsided for a few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 32826 receives Exhibit Number P7535, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32828 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Major Russell, I now want to look at the few days immediately before your meeting with Radovan Karadzic on the 3rd of January. This is a -- the sitrep from the 31st to the 1st. In section 1, during the day residential areas shelled included Sedrenik, Bare, and the city centre. We see snipers were active. One man was killed and 21 wounded, eight of which were children on the Bosnian side, and none on the Serb side. In section 2, UNMOs confirmed 149 mixed impacts incoming and two outgoing mortars from Bosnian-held areas, and 303 outgoing rounds and 23 impacts in Serb-held areas. Were you aware that even when this lower level of shelling occurred that it was having an impact on the civilian population of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, the sitrep states: "The tragedy of this war as we enter 1994 is illustrated by one family in which the man was killed, his wife critically injured, and 17-year-old son wounded." The next part indicates the casualty levels of the last two days were relatively high in relation to the number of impacts when compared to the week leading up to Christmas. Civilians were still dying on a daily basis even with this lower level of shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since you've said the civilian -- the shelling was still having an impact on civilian population of Sarajevo, what was that impact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: There was dangers in travelling across open areas of roads from both shelling and snipers. There was an effect on people trying to get food and water and any general movement around the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, the Chamber has growing concerns about the links between what the witness was called and, of course, it's not, and you would agree with that, that you would not spend whole of the time to go through the whole of the conflict again with the witness. I -- the focus of the witness still is on Markale I, credibility, reliability issues. It may be that by putting some of the questions you've touched upon them, but the Chamber does not expect you to go through all of these sitreps and to see how it developed in the war and to ask the witness about whether a hundred against ten he considered this or whether 500 against 300 he considered that, that -- so would you please keep that in mind when you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I do spend -- I plan on spending well over half of my questions related to the Markale --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not start with that, I would say. That's the focus of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I do believe that this does relate directly to the credibility of the witness. Could I tender this exhibit and then I do want to go through one more sitrep in relation to some things he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- in his testimony. The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 32828 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32828 receives Exhibit Number P7536, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go now to Exhibit -- I'm sorry, P511. And, sir, I'd like to go through, just so you understand where I'm going, a sitrep and then I'd like to look at a newspaper article, and the reason I'm doing that is because you've made some comments in terms of information being presented in the media. This is the sitrep for the 2nd to the 3rd of January, 1994. I'm going to specifically focus on a couple of items. In section 2, the UNMOs confirm 203 mixed impacts incoming and nine outgoing rounds from Bosnian-held areas, and 102 outgoing rounds and 37 impacts in Serb-held areas. At the end of the first paragraph, it also notes that a shell landed of the -- excuse me, the first section, that a shell landed 500 metres behind the Presidency, killing five members of the same family. Do you see this information before we move on to another document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I don't see that -- no, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I direct your attention back to the general assessment, towards the end of the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33011.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a "New York Times" article entitled: "Sarajevo family's fate: Shell kills 3 generations." This article discusses the death of three generations from one family on Monday, which was the 3rd of January, at about 3.30 in the afternoon, when their apartment was hit by a Howitzer shell from Mount Trebevic. In the fourth paragraph of the article it states: "The Serbian shell that destroyed Mr. Dragnic's family was one of 203 that exploded on Monday in Sarajevo, according to a United Nations tally. Beside the Dragnics, nine people were killed. The Bosnian army returned 37 shells." These totals correspond to the number of impacts from the 3 January sitrep that we just looked at; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I would think so. I mean, it's the first time I see this, and, yeah, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. We saw earlier in the meeting with Radovan Karadzic that Mr. de Mello told him: "We have been very objective in our reporting, including to the press, which he again acknowledged." You would agree that there was objective information that was provided to the international press; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Well, I would agree that the information provided by the UN comes from that information department to the press. How they do that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33011 receives Exhibit Number P7537, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7537 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32636a for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to turn to the day of the Markale shelling. This is the sitrep for the 5th of February, 1994. Directing your attention to section 2, this sitrep indicating the UNMOs confirmed 55 mixed impacts coming into Bosnian areas and zero outgoing rounds. My question: The UNMOs observed no rounds being fired by Bosnian forces on this day; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: If that's what the UN observers observed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the first sentence of section 1, there's reference to one mortar round landing on a market table. Do you understand that this information to be based on Captain Verdy's initial assessment which I think you've agreed to be -- has been shown to be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Could you direct me where that's marked, please, on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the very first sentence of the general assessment at the top.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, that would not be him. That would be a reference to -- must be my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under section 5 - and I'm just asking you if you know - the sitrep states that the SMO requested to meet the command of the BSA Sarajevo-Romanija Corps after the market shelling but this meeting was cancelled by the higher BSA authorities. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 32636a into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32636a receives Exhibit Number P7538, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just want to talk briefly about your experience with crater analysis. Prior to your training in October of 1993, you had never personally performed a crater analysis; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And in October 1993, your -- you were taken to locations where others explained to you how a crater analysis should be performed; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, the day before we had the lectures and the day after we went for practical training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. On the four previous occasions before the Markale shelling where you attended a crater analysis, were other UNMOs present on those --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Excuse me. In para 9 of the piece of paper, my statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you -- before you start reading from your own statement, if your attention is drawn to a certain part that's okay. But if you need to consult your statement in order to refresh your recollection, the Chamber would like to know that it happens. So I saw you looking at your paper, and you say: I have to look - that's how I understand it - at what I stated to refresh my recollection as to whether there were any others present. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. The crater analysis at the Egyptian Battalion, I was alone. The one at the French Battalion, I was alone. At the airport, we were normally two or three. And I know -- I can remember of one in the streets of Sarajevo, I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was the one that you attended at the airport from the 5th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that date. The dates are -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall what type of projectile -- or I'll just ask you more broadly. What kind of projectiles caused the craters on these four previous occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: They were mortar rounds. And I think they were 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That being said, the Markale market was the first time you had looked at a -- or tried to -- done a crater analysis of a larger calibre mortar, 120-millimetre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the marketplace on the 5th of February, were you aware that other analyses of the crater had already been done?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You then did not know that there was a crater analysis by the Bosnian authorities at 12.30?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I didn't know any of that stuff. I only showed up there around late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And then you would haven't known about the analysis by FreBat at 12.45 or Captain Verdy at 3.00?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you later learn about these?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yeah, when I went and finished my report, I found out that other people had been there from the UN conducting a crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And again, please pause between question and answer and the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You agree that there was only one explosion at the marketplace on the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The crater was caused by a single mortar round?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Any shrapnel fragments that would have been found on that day would have been the remnants of only one shell; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Shrapnel or shell fragments are important to determine the calibre of a mortar shell; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: More in an artillery shell. In a mortar shell, you're looking for the fin because the size of the fins give you the circumference of the calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We've heard that when you arrived that there was no shrapnel or shell fragments. You did not know the exact calibre of the projectile because you had none of these fragments available; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You would agree with me that you need to know the calibre of the shell in order to look at the appropriate range tables to determine distance, the minimum and maximum ranges; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just want to understand so we have this clearly. I want to talk to about the splash pattern. When you arrived at the market, you looked at the pattern on the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 18 of your statement when you say: "When examining the crater, I observed that the imprint left by the crater was smaller than I would have expected. This led me to believe that the round may have struck an object such as a table before hitting the ground." This is the opinion that you changed once you learned the additional information that it was embedded -- that a mortar had actually embedded into the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we just look quickly at D1221, MFI. And, Your Honours, I had originally indicated to counsel that I might be the full day. I am trying to move through rather quickly and I -- it might be the case that their next witness is needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But ... that means that you would need less than 35 minutes after the break, the break which we will take in eight minutes from now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how much time Mr. Ivetic would need for his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right now I'm looking at perhaps 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll see whether -- now, in order to -- is there any witness waiting at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None were ordered for today to be present through VWS because of the time estimates that were provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is reasonable, I would think. Mr. Weber, even if we would have five or eight minutes left, then there's no witness waiting and we're not going to organise him to be standby for five or ten minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We have had some comments on this. This is the report that you wrote after the shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The amendments in the -- you know, the handwritten ones, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so we have it clear on the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, the whole thing is after the shelling, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You initially wrote the report without the notations on the day after the shelling, on the 6th of February; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 of your statement, you indicate that you made the notations on your report sometime in the week after the explosion. Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you wrote these notations after reading the report of the UN team of experts that came several days later?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of the report, you analogize to criminal investigations of murder scenes and emphasise the importance of a site not being disturbed. Do you agree that it is best to do a crater analysis shortly after the impact in order to obtain the most reliable results?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could take the break right now, I think I would be able to reorganise and probably finish relatively efficiently after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But before we do so, I have one small question to the witness. Earlier we saw a report in which your findings were listed in a table together with other findings. Reference was made to mils there. Now in the past I learned that you have mils which are not exactly the same. Could you tell us exactly what mils you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had, Your Honour, a Silva compass, and it comes in mils.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But which kind of mils? Because mils are there in various varieties. Do you know which mils were in your compass which you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the parties are invited to seek whether they can agree on the interpretation of what kind of mils were referred to. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Russell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Major Russell, you do not remember measuring the angle of descent on the day of the Markale shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, normally, as I understand from your past testimony, you would measure the angle be reinserting a 12-inch nail into the hole of the crater?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This would allow to you obtain a generally reasonably accurate measurement of the angle of descent; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, you'd have a -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 of your statement, if you could look at it, please, you state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You state: "I do not believe that reinserting the tail-fin into the hole would provide an accurate measurement of the angle of descent since the hole had been disturbed." The fact is, is that the procedure of inserting a tail-fin would be the same as you inserting a nail into the hole; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph 22 of your statement, you comment that you were struck about how steep of an angle that the round must have come in on to clear the large building adjacent to the crater. You then state: "This led me to believe that the round had come from a location closer to the crater than a round fired from further away." I'm now going to go to your past Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 33074, e-court page 23. If I could please have page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your past Karadzic testimony, you analogize the reasoning in this paragraph to the principles of how a water hose works --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- and stated at transcript page 29396: "In the discussion I used the example of the water hose" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful to have the correct line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You explain this as: "In the discussion I used the example of the water hose, saying placing a water hose at a 45-degree angle with the maximum flow on, you would see the water fly out and then gravity would pull it down to a certain location. If you pull -- if you push the fire hose down, the area where the water lands is closer. If you pull the hose up higher than 45 degrees, the water again starts to come closer. And when I looked at the steepness of the angle of descent, this is what I was reminded of." This is how you explained your observation in the Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You wrote in your diary on the night after the shelling that you believed the BiH shot at themselves as a result of believing that a steep angle meant a closer firing range; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please now go to page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is another part of your Karadzic testimony where you were asked whether you came to an incorrect conclusion. You were asked at line 5: "Q. Do you agree with me that you applied an erroneous principle and you came to an incorrect conclusion?" Your answer: "In that particular case of the diary, yes. In the particular case of the range tables, you can see the minimum and maximum range; and therefore, those minimum and maximum ranges cross the confrontation line and that's the official report that I put in on the crater analysis." Next question: "Okay. But that's not my question. If you had understood this principle to be exactly as it's related on the firing table, and not these exact figures, but the principle that it represents, would you have come to a different conclusion than you came to in your diary? " Your answer was: "Yes." Do you stand by this testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was it during your past testimony when you were shown the range tables that you realised that you applied an incorrect principle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: The range tables that I saw were not the range tables that I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Since we're at this point in the transcript, I just want to confirm with you -- I guess I'll just read it in. When you were asked about paragraph 32 of the statement where it is -- where it was stated in the transcript here at line 18: "'That evening' -- in paragraph 32 you said you recalled hearing it reported on CNN that evening and you believed that this was a result of propaganda and that from then on it would be widely believed that the Serbs had fired the shell regardless of the true facts." "When you heard that report, that was before you wrote in your diary; correct? Your answer was: "Yes." Do you stand by this part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33075 for the witness. Page 16 in the B/C/S and page 21 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give the number again? What is the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still a bit confused, perhaps. If you say: I used different tables from the ones shown to me in the Karadzic case, in your statement I find nothing about tables being used. If I'm correct, you said you gained the impression because of the steepness of the -- where -- or were you referring to any tables you may have used when writing your official reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tables, Your Honour, that I have, or had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- were the ones that we used in the crater analysis exercise in Knin. The firing tables that were presented in the Karadzic case were firing tables of 120-millimetre Yugoslavian mortar firing table. The one I had was Soviet. So the firing tables are pretty well close. I mean, I didn't argue the firing table at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But I don't see anywhere in your statement that you used firing tables, or am I wrong? But if I'm missing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 31, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 31. Let me see...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On page 5. It's the last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there it says: "Based on the evidence available at the site, the minimum and maximum range at which the weapons system could have been fired straddles the confrontation line." It doesn't say anything about having done that, but perhaps it's included in "based on the evidence available," that's where you used the tables, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I -- yes. I understood the evidence as being what was found on the ground and not the -- the documentary materials which you used to further analyse. Yes. Did you do all those calculations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I arrived at the angle of descent, the calculations for angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to do the calculations, and looking at the firing tables, you'd need to know exactly the angle of firing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, which is -- may be related to the angle of firing, isn't it? If you fire at a steeper angle, that it falls at a steeper angle as well; whereas if you fire it at a lower angle, that it falls with a lower angle as well? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would agree in general. But you got to consider too there's wind affecting that round when it's in the air. So, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you considered wind, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I'm just stating the general principle that if you throw a ball high in the air it falls under a similar angle and if would you throw it more in a horizontal direction it also lands in a more horizon -- under a more horizontal angle. Is that a principle you would ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't get it. I don't understand, sir, what you're trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'm -- well, what I'm getting at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm confused. I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what I say is that if you throw a ball high in the air little bit forward, that is, a steep angle, then it will land, irrespective of whether there will be some wind influence, but as a general rule it will also land on a steep angle. I mean, that what's I learned in sports. And that if you throw it more horizontally, that it would also land under a more smaller angle of descent but farther away. Is that a principle would you have problems in accepting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- yes, it's okay. I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now when you applied these tables, you had no precise angle of descent, let alone a precise angle of firing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only concentrated, Your Honour, on angle of descent and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and do we find that in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's in the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And therefore I applied what I found there to the range table which told me that, based on that, it was between the confrontation lines. So I couldn't determine where -- who fired it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever do the same math again once you knew that different tables may be applicable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You took into account all the -- as you said in your statement, all the possible charges for firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Based on charge 1 to 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are they the same in all tables? Is the charges, are they --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, did you take into account possibly the difference in level of altitude from a firing position to a position where the projectile lands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to finish off today, Major Russell, I'm going to go through a similar exercise that you went through last time with the mortar table in front of you. This is the same mortar table that was shown to you during the Karadzic case. It is a firing table that corresponds to the same type of projectile that landed in the market that day, an M62P3 120-millimetre mortar shell. Do you recognise this table?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I believe that's the table I saw in the other trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you see at the -- and if I could actually -- you have the translation available to you this time. But if I could direct your attention even over to the B/C/S original of the document, do you see the boxes at the top of the table that on the page before you represent charges 1, 2, and 3, and then on the next page, there's going to be charges 4, 5, and 6?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could then please scroll back over to the left in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would like to take the angle of descent that is closest to 1200 mils as an example. I'm only using it as an example and I'm not suggesting that this was the accurate angle of descent for the mortar on the 5th. But I'm just using it since it was your estimate from that day. Going through each charge, under charge 1 the closest angle of descent is 1.218 mils. And then going across to the left to get the distance, that would be 900 metres.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Hold on now. I'm not ... the left-hand line is that the range?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first wait until we have the English version back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you at least not touch the screen. I don't know whether you did or not. But if so, please refrain from doing it. Okay. Now, slowly, Mr. Weber, and in a speed which enables ordinary people also to follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very appreciated, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to ask you to confirm if I'm reading the first one correctly and then I will read in the other ones for the other charges. Under charge 1, which would be in the -- the left-hand side of the original before you, if you go into the third column in the chart, under angle of descent, the closest angle of descent I see to the one that you estimated was 1.218 mils which then going across to the left to the far left column, that would correspond to a distance of 900 metres?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you I oriented you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Now I got the way it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Well, I think the range on the left side? The distance is on the left-hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The distance is in metres.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: In metres on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What does VD stand for, Mr. -- we have a table with range finder graduation, angle of descent, and VD. And that's all related to a distance. What does VD --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd have to get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what VD stands for in his view.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to assist us at all with what the notation VD stands for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And just so I get to know what your understanding is here, under the first charge we see that there's a Vo 128 M/S. Do you realise that that relates to the velocity in distance metres per second?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- I understand that metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do we also agree that Vo is the initial, the speed at firing? At time zero?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So we have a complete record, under the second charge, we have the closest one being 1.198 mils. And at that charge for the shell we go over to get the distance and that would be 1700 metres. For the third charge, we have 1.203 mils as being the closest. And for that distance, that would fire the shell at 2500 metres --

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could go over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the fourth charge, 1.202 mils, that would fire the projectile 3.300 metres.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The fifth is 1.198 mils, I see is the closest one, which would end up being 4.100 metres. And the sixth charge, the closest measurement in terms of angle of descent to yours would be 1.192 mils. That's 1.192 mils which would end up an a distance of 4.800 metres. Have I read this correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I'm in agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. After seeing this table yet again, your assumption that you made on the evening of the 5th was incorrect because the fact is you can have similar angles of descent for projectiles fired from different ranges based on the number of charges that are used; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that you have considered that already in your statement, isn't it? In a general way. You are talking about the charges and that you say that may have an impact. But did you then not -- let me just ... if the parties could assist me whether I do remember that the witness ... I'm sorry that I cannot find it immediately. Okay. I'll try to find it to see whether you had already considered that when you made your assessment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last answer of the witness was not recorded. Perhaps you can clarify, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 23, I think, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just so we have clarity I'll repeat the full question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After seeing this table yet again, your assumption that you made on the evening of the 5th was incorrect because the fact is you can have similar angles of descent for projectiles fired from different ranges based on the number of charges that are used; right? That is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object as it's vague. If he is talking about an assumption, he needs to identify which assumption or which conclusion he's making reference to so the gentleman knows what to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if it would -- I think the question was sufficiently clear, but perhaps if Mr. Ivetic would like to have it more precise, then you rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, the assumption that I'm referring to is the assumption you made about the BiH firing on themselves.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: So the assumption in the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: You are correct, that is a personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And based on the firing tables, you appreciate that it is incorrect, that assumption?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Based on the firing tables, I believe that the round could have been fired from any side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. It could have -- right. So are you agreeing that the assumption that you made is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: I'm saying that what I personally recorded in my diary is what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any room for belief there. I mean, I can believe that -- whatever I want which has got nothing to do with reality. Would you agree with me, then, that what you believed at the time was not based on any calculations or any conclusions that could be verified by other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So subject --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Subjective --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not objective.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in your training in October 1993, and in the ten or so times that you've done an analysis, the speed of the mortar is something that you've never considered; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And we've now gone and looked at this table. If I could direct your attention back to it, we -- you can see it in the translation where in the first charge the speed is 128 metres per second outgoing and you can see, for example, down in the fourth charge that it's almost twice that velocity of 250 metres per second. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN RUSSELL
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
